list.listitem: Obtain neuroimaging on patients with suspicious findings on neurological examination, altered mental status that is otherwise unexplained, or with symptoms or signs of increased neurological pressure. C

The extent of extracranial disease and the number of CNS lesions will determine whether patients with brain metastases should be treated with whole brain radiotherapy alone, a combination of whole brain radiotherapy and either surgery or radiosurgery, or (rarely) surgery or radiosurgery alone. A
Patients with primary malignant gliomas are treated with surgery followed by radiotherapy with concurrent and adjuvant temozolomide. A

background.definition: Malignant brain tumors include primary tumors arising from various cell types in the central nervous system (CNS) that are high grade (ie, World Health Organization grade III or grade IV), as well as metastatic tumors from non-CNS primary tumors. The majority of malignant brain tumors in adults consist of metastases or malignant gliomas.

list.listitem: The incidence rate for primary malignant brain tumors is estimated to be 0.074 per 1000 persons per year by the Central Brain Tumor Registry of the United States.
The incidence of brain metastasis varies by primary tumor site.
The estimated prevalence of primary malignant brain tumors is approximately 0.3 per 1000 persons.
Genetic predisposition (for primary malignant brain tumors).
Ionizing radiation (greater risk for benign than malignant primary brain tumors).
Non-CNS malignancy (for metastatic malignant brain tumors).
Cell phones do not appear to increase the risk of brain tumor.
Primary tumors generally grow locally. Some will metastasize along the neuraxis.
Extra-CNS metastasis is rare for primary malignant brain tumors.

Consider prophylactic cranial irradiation (PCI) to prevent brain metastases for patients with limited-stage small-cell lung cancer who have achieved a complete response. An updated Cochrane review of PCI in small cell lung cancer with 987 patients demonstrates not just reduced incidence subsequent brain metastases but significant benefit in three year overall survival. A
Patients with extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer also benefit from prophylactic cranial irradiation. B
Insufficient data exist to support prophylactic cranial irradiation in patients with nonsmall-cell lung cancer. B
Screening for metastatic brain tumors depends on patient factors including symptoms and primary tumor. C
History and physical examination may reveal focal neurological deficits and/or signs or symptoms of increased neurological pressure. C
Obtain neuroimaging in adults and children with new focal neurological deficits and/or signs or symptoms of increased neurological pressure, and in children with suspicious headaches. B
Patients may present with abnormal headaches.

Focal neurological deficit(s) on physical examination and evidence of papilledema increase the likelihood of intracranial mass (LR+ = 12 and 4.1, respectively) and warrant a workup with neuroimaging. A systematic review identified abnormal findings on neurological examination,headache not fitting migraine, cluster, or tension-type definition, and aura as the best predictors of significant intracranial abnormality.
In addition, patients presenting with altered mentation should receive neuroimaging unless another reversible cause for their altered mentation is found.

Another systematic review identified six studies of over 150,000 symptomatic patients in primary care to determine the positive predictive value of symptoms for brain and CNS cancer. They found that new onset seizure was the only item with a PPV greater than 1% in adults; it was 2.3% in patients age 60 to 69 years. Symptom combinations were similarly unhelpful.

Obtain neuroimaging in adults and children with new focal neurological deficits and/or signs or symptoms of increased neurological pressure, and in children with suspicious headaches. American College of Radiology guidelines recommend CT or MRI in children, and MRI with and without contrast is slightly preferred to CT in adults.

Advancing techniques in MR imaging are improving ability of imaging to differentiate grades and types of brain tumours. Specifically, diffusion weighted MR scanning can better distinguish low grade from high grade gliomas. It is also helpful in distinguishing response after radiotherapy in differentiating pseudoprogression from true progression of disease.

Techniques using MRI scoring in tumours which lack contrast enhancement may help to predict biological characeteristics to guide treatment in patients with glioma. (IDH mutation and 1p/19q co-deletion).
In patients with a known extracranial malignancy and signs or symptoms of increased intracranial pressure, a CT or MRI of the brain is also appropriate.

Patients with signs or symptoms of spinal disease and/or with histologies at high risk of CNS dissemination (such as medulloblastoma) should undergo imaging of the entire spine, as well as lumbar puncture with cerebrospinal fluid cytology.

A systematic review of 18 studies with 1172 patients concluded that apparent diffusion coefficients (ADC) of diffusion weighted MRI has good accuracy for distinguishing high grade from low-grade gliomas, with LR+ 6.1 and LR- 0.22.
Patients with a CNS lesion should first have a careful evaluation for systemic disease (ie, a non-CNS primary tumor).

If that evaluation is negative, the CNS lesion should be biopsied. If the evaluation identifies a peripheral lesion, that lesion should be biopsied if possible before considering biopsy of the CNS lesion.
See Treatment section for recommended treatment of primary CNS and metastatic CNS lesions.
Single metastasis: resection followed by whole brain radiotherapy, or whole brain radiotherapy followed by stereotactic radiosurgery. A

One to 3 brain metastases: whole brain radiotherapy with or without stereotactic radiosurgery; 4 or more brain metastases: whole brain radiotherapy alone. The use of whole brain radiotherapy depends on the patient's prognosis, and is associated with an increased likelihood of cognitive decline and reduced quality of life compared to radiosurgery alone. A
Primary glioblastoma: biopsy or resection followed by radiotherapy with concurrent and adjuvant temozolomide. A
Primary anaplastic astrocytoma: maximal safe resection followed by radiotherapy with concurrent and adjuvant temozolomide. C

The most recent American Society for Radiation Oncology (ASTRO) guidelines distinguish between the need for post-operative radiotherapy in grade 2 and 3 gliomas in patients with IDH mutation depending upon other risk factors. For the IDH mutation with 1p/19q co-deletion (both are good prognostic indicators) then in the absence of any other high risk features G2 gliomas should have observation follow-up omitting radiotherapy. Radiotherapy is indicated for oligodendroglioma (grade 3).

Patients with signs of increased intracranial pressure and evidence of a brain tumor on imaging studies should be given corticosteroids.. to reduce intracranial pressure. The steroids must be slowly tapered at the end of treatment, though some patients with residual disease are unable to tolerate steroid taper.

Patients with brain tumors, either primary or metastatic, should not be given prophylactic anticonvulsants. If patients present with seizures or develop seizures, then it is appropriate to give them anticonvulsants. Clinical trials regarding choice of anticonvulsant are lacking. A single study compared levetiracetam with phenytoin and found that the former was at least as effective (87% vs 75% seizure free at 6 months). Note that some anticonvulsants (enzyme inducing anti-epileptics such as phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, or phenobarbital) interact with the corticosteroids that a majority of these patients are taking and may reduce their levels.

Many patients with primary malignant brain tumors receive chemotherapy as a part of their treatment. A systematic review of 12 RCTs found that chemotherapy for high-grade glioma improved survival. A detailed discussion is beyond the scope of this chapter. For current guidelines on clinicians should refer to NCCN guidelines for CNS cancers. Early progression on MRI is a predictor of a poor response.

For primary brain tumours a Cochrane review found two RCTs comparing insertion of a carmustine impregnated wafer in the resection cavity with placebo wafer. The chemotherapy impregnated wafer improved survival (HR 0.65; 95% CI, 0.48-0.86) for primary disease, but not for recurrent disease.

Temozolomide has been shown to improve outcomes and is endorsed by NICE guidelines for fit patients with newly diagnosed glioblastoma multiforme. In addition, a randomized trial in 562 patients 70 and older with glioblastoma found that temozolomide added to standard radiation therapy is effective, with increased median survival (13.5 vs 7.7 months, p <0.001).

In patients with progressive glioblastoma, single agent lomustine is effective. A recent RCT concluded that addition of bevacizumab to lomustine did not improve survival further and contributed to increased toxicity.
There is now evidence that in young patients with resected low grade gliomas, there is significant survival advantage from the addition of chemotherapy to post-operative radiotherapy.
Evidence is lacking regarding drug therapy for depression in patients with brain tumor.
Maximal safe resection is desirable for most primary malignant brain tumors. This was supported by a 2012 observational study showing better survival in patients with more than 90% tumor resection.

A Cochrane review seeking to update whether resection is better than biopsy for high grade glioma confirms that there are still no adequate trials to address this but there is an ongoing study which may contribute to the evidence.

A recent meta-analysis of the relationship between the extent of resection and subsequent survival in GBM wild type IDH mutation demonstrated in a combined population of 2023 patients from 9 trials, a significant increase in median overall survival from 12 to 20 months for gross total resection compared to subtotal resection.

Similarly a systematic review of 234 patients with diffuse low grade glioma demonstrated improved functional outcomes assessed by return to work within one year for patients receiving gross total resection compared to subtotal resection, which was in turn better than partial resection.

5-ALA fluorescence guided surgery has been demonstrated to improve success of gross tumour resection (GTR). In the RESECT study of 171 patients GTR was achieved in 79% patients with 5-ALA guided resection compared to 48% without 5-ALA. On short follow-up this did not translate into improved overall survival, though.
A systematic review of 68 observational studies suggested an association between preoperative brain mapping using functional MRI to plan resection and reduced morbidity.

A study compared overall and progression free survival in 145 patients stratified by the time from diagnostic MRI to surgery (< 7, 7 to 21, and > 21 days). It found no significant differences between groups.

Use of NSAIDs post-operatively appears to be relatively safe. A study identified 1182 patients with normal renal function who had undergone craniotomy for brain malignancy, of whom 114 received an NSAID within 48 hours of surgery. They found that return to the OR for bleeding occured in 1 or 114 who got an NSAID and 3 of 1068 who did not (RR 3.1, 95% CI 0.33-30).
Adjuvant or definitive radiotherapy plays a role in the management of most primary malignant brain tumors and nearly all metastatic malignant brain tumors.

Standard of care radiotherapy in GBM patients is the Stupp regimen delivering 60Gy over 6 weeks which is difficult for frail patients. These have traditionally received shorter course 3 week radiotherapy but there is a case to consider increasing the dose even within the 3 week schedule to achieve better control in this group.

In patients with a single brain metastasis, resection followed by whole brain radiotherapy, or whole brain radiotherapy followed by stereotactic radiosurgery is appropriate in most situations. A systematic review of 3 RCTs with 195 patients found no difference in overall survival for surgery plus whole brain radiotherapy compared with whole brain radiotherapy alone. However, there was improved functionally independent survival and no difference in adverse events.
In patients with 1 to 3 brain metastases, whole brain radiotherapy followed by stereotactic radiosurgery is appropriate.
In patients with 4 or more brain metastases, whole brain radiotherapy alone is appropriate, usually given in 10 to 15 treatments to a total dose of 3000 to 3750 cGy.

The use of whole brain radiotherapy in brain metastases will depend upon the primary site of tumour and the patient's prognosis. It is increasingly influenced by evidence of reduced quality of life and early cognitive decline associated with whole brain treatment. In a recent trial using radiosurgery alone or with the addition of whole brain radiation, there was less cognitive decline and better quality of life in the group without whole brain radiation.

A large phase 3 RCT in non-small cell lung cancer compared optimal supportive care alone with the addition of whole brain radiation for brain metastases and found no improvement in survival or quality of life with radiotherapy.

In glioblastomas (World Health Organization grade IV malignant gliomas), the combination of temozolomide with radiotherapy confers a survival advantage versus radiotherapy alone. An RCT randomized 291 patients over age 60 years to temozolomide (200 mg/m2), hypofractionated radiotherapy, or standard radiotherapy. Outcomes (including survival) were worse in those receiving standard radiotherapy, especially among patients over 70 years of age.
Although a randomized trial is lacking, temozolomide is often given concurrently with radiotherapy to patients with anaplastic astrocytomas (World Health Organization grade III malignant gliomas).
In recurrent glioblastoma, if small volume disease in a patient with good performance status, there may be a survival benefit with use of salvage stereotactic radiosurgery.

For patients with primary malignant gliomas, a Radiation Therapy Oncology Group recursive partitioning analysis classification exists that indicates a patient's estimated median survival on the basis of their characteristics (see ). B

The use of molecular biomarkers can guide prognostication. In glioblastoma there is evidence that MGMT methylation and IDH1 mutation each separately confer better overall survival. In contrast EGFR gene overexpression or amplification does not.
A similar classification exists for patients with brain metastases (see ). B

For primary brain tumors, patients should be followed with neuroimaging (likely MRI) every 3 to 4 months for 1 to 2 years, every 6 months for 2 to 3 years, then yearly if symptoms and imaging studies remain stable. C
In follow-up imaging it may be challenging to distinguish recurrence from radiation necrosis. A meta-analysis of 9 trial (354 patients) suggests MR spectroscopy can be used in this situation.

For patients with metastatic brain tumors, the choice to repeat neuroimaging and the interval at which this is done should be based on the likelihood of obtaining useful information that can be acted on for the patient's benefit. C

A systematic review identified 10 studies of 101 patients with intracranial extraventricular neurocytomas. The 5 year rate of overall survival was 90% and progression free survival was 49%. Patients under age 50 had better survival.
Some experts have speculated that there is no benefit to treating older patients with malignant brain tumors. However, recent studies show some benefit to treatment in this patient population.
Primary malignant brain tumors in children represent a special challenge since children are especially sensitive to the neurocognitive effects of radiotherapy.
Treatments generally involve a combination of surgery, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy.
Long-term follow up is essential since late side effects of therapy are a significant problem for these patients.

I-II Anaplastic astrocytoma, KPS 70-100, symptoms present >3 months 40-60

Glioblastoma, age <50 years, KPS 70-100
V-VI Glioblastoma and age >50 years 5-9
Glioblastoma or anaplastic astrocytoma, KPS <70
KPS denotes Karnosfsky Performance Score; score of 60, requires occasional assistance, but is able to care for most personal needs; score of 70, cares for self, but unable to carry on normal activity or do active work.
